newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya shilling down on panic, seen losing further.
newsitem.headline: Kenya shilling down on panic, seen losing further.

text.p: The Central Bank of Kenya's (CBK) Governor Micah Cheserem said on Wednesday that the shilling had taken a beating due to market jitters following political unrest on Monday but the phenomenon was temporary.
"This is a temporary panic. I believe what we saw on July 7 will not be repeated," Cheserem told Reuters.

The shilling slipped to around 56.50/65 versus the dollar on Wednesday compared with a 54.90 close on Friday last week. The shilling fell to a commercial mean rate of 55.32 against the dollar on Monday and fell back to 55.35 on Tuesday.
Against the pound, the shilling was traded at a mean rate of 93.39, steady at 93.34 on Tuesday and 94.36 on Wednesday.

Nine people were killed in Kenya on Monday during the most violent clashes between police and protesters since unrest in 1990 that helped push Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi to allow multi-party elections.

"Our view is that soon the authorities will begin dialogue with whoever is concerned (so that conflict does not escalate). What we have seen will not be repeated. Sanity will prevail," the governor added.
Leading currency traders said the shilling was poised to weaken if the political tension in the country dragged on.
They added that many of their offshore clients had already expressed an interest in pulling out of the market.
"It looks like it will weaken further. (Foreign investors) are getting jittery and are scared of losing on their interest gains," one dealer said.
Another dealer added that more demand from nervous importers who were buying dollars forward to hedge against exchange rate losses had put more pressure on the shilling to weaken.
Cheserem said he understood investor concerns over the violence on Monday but was confident that the government would do all in its powers to ensure peace and stability prevailed.
"If there were lasting problems, I would be the first to advise investors. The situation is calming and the temporary panic should be reversed in the coming days," he said.
Cheserem said that the central bank had "some dollars" to intervene if the shilling depreciated on panic or jitters over an uncertain future rather than fundamentals.
"We would like the shilling to depreciate on fundamentals. As you know some people hold that the shilling is rather overvalued," Cheserem added.

Traders said worries about the ability of the interbank market to meet dollar demand due to the suspension of coffee export auctions for two weeks due to acute shortages had aggravated the already jittery market.
Coffee is the country's main foreign exchange earner.
